title: How this lesson works
text: Before you start · your group ≈ 2 min How this lesson works Slideshow lead Reads each slide aloud and moves the deck forward. Whiteboard scribe Holds the dry erase marker and works problems at the whiteboard. Timekeeper · support Starts each timer and keeps the group on pace. Checker · support Asks "How do we know?" before anyone presses Show answer. Explicit instruction Read it together. Then one person restates it in their own words. Check your understanding Solve alone, compare answers, agree — then press Show answer. Group tasks Start the timer. Everyone contributes before you move on. Exit ticket On your own. Submit it with this lesson's assignment. Day 6 · Vector Addition Antocci Physics · 02 / 30 2 students: lead + timekeeper, scribe + checker. 3 students: third person takes both support duties. Roles rotate at each discussion. Everyone submits their own work.

title: Rebuild the fictional velocity
text: 2026-XJ · The Arrow Test · Graphic novel, page 24 Rebuild the fictional velocity The classroom model points positive x away from Earth. The velocity components are negative 8210 meters per second in x and positive 2200 in y. They give speed about 8500 meters per second and direction about 15 degrees from toward Earth toward positive y. With +x away from Earth, vₓ = −8,210 m/s and vᵧ = +2,200 m/s. Why is the direction about 165° from +x, rather than 15° from +x? Part 2 · Check components and direction · Write your own answer in Work. Fictional story · Original artwork · Day 6

title: Check the angle before choosing sine or cosine
text: 2026-XJ · The Arrow Test · Graphic novel, page 23 Check the angle before choosing sine or cosine The same ten-meter-per-second vector is shown 30 degrees above horizontal, equivalently 60 degrees from vertical. Its components stay 8.66 horizontally and 5 vertically. Mr. Antocci explains that cosine belongs to the component beside the marked angle. Changing the reference angle does not change the arrow. Cosine goes with the adjacent component. How can both angle descriptions produce the same two components? Part 3 · Defend your reference angle · Write your own answer in Work.
